title: Reply to the major: what cannot be demonstrated can still be faith's first rule
source_text: XXIV. Ad majorem vero illam, Quod ex se nobis est dubium & incertum firma fide non potest apprehendi, & esse certa fidei regula, nisi authoritate superiore confirmetur. Resp. falsissimam esse, si per illud quod nobis est incertum intelligatur id quod demonstrari non potest, & argumentis prorsus necessariis confirmari. Etenim quod probari non potest argumentis, philosophice & proprie loquendo, necessariis & evidentibus, firma tamen fide potest apprehendi, & esse certa fidei regula, quamvis authoritate quoad nos superiori & priori non confirmetur. Imo, ut jamjam probavimus, omnino necesse est ut prima fidei regula sit aliquid inevidens, quod demonstrari non possit, nec tamen superiori authoritate confirmari aut queat aut debeat. Quandoquidem hoc pacto non esset, ut supponitur, prima & suprema fidei regula, sed subalterna tantum & inferior.
pass_a_gloss: But to that major, What of itself is doubtful and uncertain to us cannot be apprehended with firm faith, and be a certain rule of faith, unless it is confirmed by a superior authority. Reply: it is most false, if by that which is uncertain to us is understood that which cannot be demonstrated, and confirmed by arguments altogether necessary. For what cannot be proved by arguments necessary and evident, speaking philosophically and properly, can nevertheless be apprehended with firm faith, and be a certain rule of faith, even though it is not confirmed by an authority superior and prior with respect to us. Indeed, as we have just proved, it is altogether necessary that the first rule of faith be something non-evident, which cannot be demonstrated, and yet neither can nor ought to be confirmed by a superior authority. Since by this arrangement it would not be, as is supposed, the first and supreme rule of faith, but only subaltern and inferior.
pass_b_english: As for the major — that what is doubtful and uncertain to us of itself cannot be firmly grasped or stand as a sure rule of faith unless a higher authority confirms it — the reply is that this is utterly false if "uncertain to us" means "what cannot be demonstrated and confirmed by wholly necessary arguments."

What cannot be proved by necessary and evident arguments in the philosophical sense can still be firmly believed and be a sure rule of faith, even without confirmation from an authority prior and superior for us.

As we have just shown, the first rule of faith must be something non-evident that cannot be demonstrated — and that neither can nor should be confirmed by a higher authority. Otherwise it would not be, as supposed, faith's first and supreme rule, but only a subordinate, inferior one.

choices.why: Not supreme if confirmed by a higher rule.
